 Florida dengue outbreak grows by 100 cases in one week, surges to 624 
 By Cheryl McCloud and C. A. Bridges, USA TODAY NETWORK - Florida 
 USA Today Network via Reuters Connect 
 Updated November 13, 2026 4:04 PM 
 The Nov. 1-7, 2026 arbovirus surveillance report from the Florida Department of Health.
 Provided by Florida Department o
 USA TODAY Network, Reuters 
 The historic surge in dengue fever is getting worse. Florida reported 100 more locally acquired cases in one week, according to the latest update from the Florida Department of Health.
 The mosquito-borne disease is also called breakbone fever, due to the pain it causes.
 That brings the statewide total for the year to 624 as of Nov. 7, the largest outbreak in the United States in decades. The previous record for Florida cases in recent memory was 199 in 2023. In 2025, Florida reported 62 cases.
 The numbers may climb even higher in the weeks ahead after record rainfall left roads flooded, ditches full, and standing water in many Florida yards.
 ➤ Prevent dengue at home in Florida with this 10-minute mosquito inspection
 The bulk of the cases continues to be in Hillsborough County on Florida's west coast, which now has 468 confirmed cases. Nearby Pinellas County is now up to 109 cases. Locally acquired cases have been reported in 12 counties.
 The outbreak prompted Hillsborough County Administrator Bonnie Wise to issue a state of local emergency, which expires Nov. 19 unless the county extends it again as officials "work to control the mosquito population and protect residents from dengue fever."
 One death has been confirmed in Hillsborough County, identified as 80-year-old Gay Small, who died of "dengue infection" along with septic shock and multi-organ failure, according to a death certificate.
 Florida's outbreak far exceeds the previous largest outbreak, which was 264 local cases in Hawaii's Big Island between September 2015 and March 2016.
 President Trump in September issued an order for a "campaign" to reduce the mosquito and tick population in Washington, D.C. That model could then be "applied as targeted, innovative, non-chemical pest control for the whole nation."
 Dengue isn't the only mosquito-transmitted disease that has been this year in Florida, although those have been in far fewer numbers than dengue: West Nile Virus, Chikungunya and Eastern Equine Encephalitis. Another case each of West Nile and Chikungunya was reported last week.
 Here's what you should know about mosquito-borne illnesses in Florida, symptoms to watch for, and how best to prevent mosquito bites, including advice from the Florida Department of Health.
 21 counties under mosquito-borne illness advisories, alerts
 A mosquito-borne illness advisory has been issued for the following counties:
 Bay
 Brevard
 Broward
 Columbia
 Holmes
 Leon
 Manatee
 Martin
 Palm Beach
 Polk
 Sarasota
 Walton
 A mosquito-borne illness alert has been issued for the following counties:
 Alachua
 Citrus
 Duval
 Hillsborough
 Miami-Dade
 Orange
 Pasco
 Pinellas
 Seminole
 "A mosquito-borne illness advisory means the public should take precautions to reduce mosquito bites due to factors indicating local disease such as positive sentinels, very few presumptive or positive human cases, or other justifications," according to Sarasota County.
 "A mosquito-borne illness alert means that there has been heightened disease activity, a significant increase in vector (disease-capable) mosquito populations, or an increase in locally-transmitted human cases.
 "Residents should continue to take precautions, but exercise additional caution in preventing mosquito bites."
 Dengue cases continue to climb in Florida
 According to Florida Department of Health data released Nov. 13, 12 counties have reported 624 locally acquired dengue cases, up from 524 reported Nov. 6.
 There have also been nine positive samples of locally acquired West Nile virus and two cases of chikungunya.
 Dengue: 624 cases 468 in Hillsborough County
 109 in Pinellas County
 16 in Miami-Dade County
 14 in Orange County
 6 in Pasco County
 3 in Citrus County
 2 in Manatee County
 2 in Seminole County
 1 in Brevard County 
 1 in Broward County
 1 in Palm Beach County
 1 in Polk County
 West Nile: nine cases 2 in Alachua County
 2 in Duval County (including one asymptomatic blood donor)
 1 in Columbia County
 1 in Holmes County
 1 in Leon (asymptomatic blood donor)
 1 in Sarasota County
 1 in Walton County
 Chikungunya: 2 cases 2 in Miami-Dade County
 Eastern Equine Encephalitis: 1 case 1 in Leon County
 Florida health officials have also reported 422 cases of dengue in victims who traveled from a dengue-endemic area within two weeks of onset. Counties reporting international-travel-associated cases were: Alachua, Bay, Brevard (4), Broward (20), Collier (5), Duval (3), Hendry, Hernando, Hillsborough (26), Lake, Lee (19), Manatee (3), Marion (2), Miami-Dade (271), Monroe (3), Orange (8), Osceola (3), Palm Beach (20), Pasco (3), Pinellas (4), Polk (4), Sarasota (2), Seminole (4), St. Johns (4), St. Lucie (8), and Walton. Six cases were reported in non-Florida residents.
 What is Hillsborough County doing to try to control mosquitoes?
 "Mosquito management crews are increasing treatments by air and ground because the county's mosquito surveillance in many neighborhoods is showing dengue virus activity in the mosquito population.
 "Residents are encouraged to look for and eliminate standing water on their property after recent heavy rains."
 Residents can sign up to be notified where aerial treatment will occur in neighborhoods.
 You can also go to the county's website to see when and where mosquito "operations" are scheduled to take place. 
 Florida residents should take precautions to avoid mosquito-borne illnesses
 "Residents throughout the state should continue to take precautions from mosquito-borne illnesses by appropriately applying bug spray, avoiding areas with high mosquito populations, and wearing long pants and shirts when possible - especially during sunrise and sunset when mosquitos are most active," said Isabella White, FDOH press secretary via email Sept. 23. 
 White said FDOH "continues to coordinate with local mosquito control partners to support surveillance and targeted response efforts in affected areas. These efforts help reduce mosquito populations, limit the risk of disease transmission, and protect residents across Florida." 
 What are symptoms of dengue, breakbone fever?
 "Dengue fever can be a painful, debilitating disease but is rarely fatal," the Florida Department of Health said. Symptoms appear three to 14 days after the bite of an infected mosquito and include:
 sudden onset of fever
 severe headache
 eye pain
 muscle and joint pain (giving the disease the nickname "breakbone fever")
 bleeding
 Gastrointestinal symptoms like vomiting and diarrhea may also be present in some cases.
 "Dengue fever symptoms usually last four to seven days. The disease is often diagnosed incorrectly because the symptoms are similar to influenza and other viruses," the CDC said.
 "Around one out of every 20 people infected by a dengue virus develops severe dengue, a life-threatening medical emergency that requires immediate medical attention," according to YaleMedicine.
 Why is dengue called 'breakbone fever?'
 Dengue is sometimes called "breakbone fever" because, in addition to fever, "it can cause severe aches and pains, especially in the legs, joints, and back," according to YaleMedicine.
 Dengue does not actually cause bones to break, according to YaleMedicine.
 Is dengue contagious?
 Dengue is spread by mosquitoes. Mosquitoes become infected with dengue after biting a person with the virus. Those infected mosquitoes then spread the virus to other people through bites.
 The Centers for Disease Control said a woman infected with the dengue virus during pregnancy could pass the virus to her fetus, causing death to the fetus, low birth weight, or premature birth.
 Can dengue be treated?
 "While there is no cure for dengue and there are no specific medications for the condition, getting adequate hydration and plenty of rest, and taking acetaminophen for pain and fever can help alleviate symptoms while the body's immune system fights the virus," according to YaleMedicine.
 "In most cases, people recover from dengue within a week. For those with severe dengue, treatment by health care professionals can significantly lower the risk of death."
 What are the best mosquito repellents to use?
 According to the Florida Department of Health, repellents with the following active ingredients provide the best protection:
 DEET
 Picaridin
 IR3535
 Oil of lemon eucalyptus
 Para-menthane-diol
 2-undecanone, a plant-derived ingredient
 'Drain and cover' helps keep mosquitoes away
 The FDOH offered this advice to help keep mosquitoes away from your Florida home:
 Drain
 Drain water from garbage cans, old tires, pool covers, or any other containers where water collects.
 Empty and clean birdbaths and pet water bowls at least once or twice a week.
 Protect boats and vehicles from rain with tarps that don't accumulate water.
 Maintain swimming pools in good condition and ensure they are appropriately chlorinated.
 Empty plastic swimming pools when not in use.
 Cover
 If you must be outside when mosquitoes are active, cover up.
 Apply mosquito repellent to exposed skin and clothing.
 Use mosquito netting to protect children younger than 2 months old.
